content.title: Which co-benefit of sustainable energy is most likely to influence local community well-being?

options.value: Reduced air pollution leading to better health outcomes
Increased energy cost savings for households
Creation of new technical job opportunities

takeaways.title: Diverse Renewable Technologies are Key to Emission Reductions.
takeaways.description: Solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, and hydrogen are playing a crucial role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and accelerating the global energy transition. Each technology has unique advantages, such as solar PV’s affordability, wind energy’s scalability, hydropower’s grid stability, geothermal’s reliability, and hydrogen’s potential for hard-to-abate sectors.

takeaways.title: Implementation Challenges Must Be Addressed.
takeaways.description: While renewable energy technologies offer significant benefits, their implementation faces challenges, including high initial investment costs, grid integration issues, financing constraints, and infrastructure limitations, particularly in developing countries.

takeaways.title: Strategic Approaches are Essential for Scaling Renewable Energy.
takeaways.description: Policy incentives, innovative financing (e.g., blended finance and concessional loans), infrastructure development (grid modernization and energy storage), capacity building, and community engagement are key strategies for scaling up renewable energy deployment, ensuring equitable access, and supporting a just energy transition.

content.text:
Gender Empowerment and the clean cooking 💬️ Crisis
The transition to sustainable energy has profound implications for gender equity. Women and girls bear the brunt of "energy poverty," spending an average of 1.4 hours per day collecting solid fuels for cooking. This task, combined with the health impacts of household air pollution, costs the global economy US$1.4 trillion annually, with women bearing a disproportionate share of US$0.8 trillion.
Expanding access to clean cooking technologies (biogas, electric cooking) and decentralized solar systems allows women to redirect their time toward education, leisure, and entrepreneurship. Programs like Panama's "Solar Champions" specifically train Indigenous women to install and maintain solar PV systems, creating new career pathways in traditionally male-dominated sectors. Furthermore, women represent 32% of the renewable energy workforce, significantly higher than the 22% found in the oil and gas sector, indicating that the green transition is inherently more inclusive.

For the 666 million people globally without electricity, the sustainable energy transition is primarily a tool for human development and poverty alleviation. Access to modern energy is a fundamental enabler of other SDGs, including education, clean water, and gender equality.
Closing the Energy Access Gap in Remote Regions
Decentralized renewable energy (DRE) solutions, such as mini-grids and off-grid solar systems, are the most rapid and cost-effective means of providing power to remote populations.35 Between 2020 and 2022, off-grid solar accounted for 55% of all new electricity connections in Sub-Saharan Africa. In Tanzania, electricity access more than tripled in a decade, rising from 14% in 2011 to 46% in 2022, driven largely by solar deployment.
Electrification of healthcare facilities is another critical social co-benefit. One in ten facilities in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa currently lacks electricity; providing reliable solar power is essential for refrigeration of vaccines, operation of life-saving equipment, and implementation of digital health systems.

Employment Generation and the Skill Premium
Renewable energy is a more labor-intensive sector than the traditional fossil fuel industry. In 2023, global clean energy employment reached 34.8 million, with 16.2 million jobs directly in renewables. Solar PV alone accounts for 44% of the total renewable workforce.38 Crucially for developing economies, nearly half of all new energy jobs created by 2030 will be in construction and installation, which offer accessible entry points for local labor.
In South Africa, green energy jobs already command a wage premium, with salaries 16% higher than those in other sectors. Projects like Nigeria's "Solar Power Naija" aim to create 250,000 jobs by providing solar home systems 💬️ to 5 million households while supporting local assembly and manufacturing worth US$10 million annually in import substitution

Renewable energy is a more labor-intensive sector than the traditional fossil fuel industry. In 2023, global clean energy employment reached 34.8 million, with 16.2 million jobs directly in renewables. Solar PV alone accounts for 44% of the total renewable workforce.38 Crucially for developing economies, nearly half of all new energy jobs created by 2030 will be in construction and installation, which offer accessible entry points for local labor.
In South Africa, green energy jobs already command a wage premium, with salaries 16% higher than those in other sectors. Projects like Nigeria's "Solar Power Naija" aim to create 250,000 jobs by providing solar home systems to 5 million households while supporting local assembly and manufacturing worth US$10 million annually in import substitution

The economic rationale for sustainable energy in developing countries has moved beyond subsidized pilot projects to a core driver of GDP growth and industrial modernization. Investing in renewable energy delivers an outsized economic multiplier; every dollar invested is estimated to return four dollars in health, food security, and education benefits.
Macroeconomic Benefits and GDP Productivity
Between 2017 and 2022, climate finance flows increased the GDP of the 100 largest low- and middle-income countries by an aggregate of US 1.2 trillion, representing a growth contributions of 1.2 trillion. Developing economies possess a "leapfrogging" advantage, as they can bypass the high costs of maintaining legacy fossil fuel infrastructure and move directly to decentralized, digitalized grids. Under rapid transition scenarios, energy-sector total factor productivity (TFP) in EMDEs could double within 25 years. This energy-sector boost is projected to drive economy-wide GDP gains as high as 9–12% for countries such as Burundi, DR Congo, and Mozambique, providing a structural advantage in a net-zero global economy.

Solar purification units installed in Iraq’s Al Hawizeh marshlands deliver safe drinking water while strengthening local governance and reducing gendered burdens (UNDP, 2021)
In the southern marshlands of Iraq, climate change is not a future threat; it is a daily destabilizer of the environment. Water scarcity, land degradation, and rising temperatures have undermined livelihoods and deepened fragility, particularly in the Al Hawizeh region. Communities already displaced by conflict face an added risk: being forced to migrate again, this time not by war but by drought. Women and children are hit the hardest, walking farther for water, losing access to income, and living in unhealthy conditions worsened by failing sanitation. In Iraq, the climate crisis has become a human security emergency (UNDP, 2021).
To respond, the UNDP-led ‘Climate Action for Human Security’ initiative delivered more than infrastructure; it delivered agency. With funding from the SDG Climate Facility, the project provided clean energy and water solutions to vulnerable communities, restoring livelihoods and enhancing local governance (UNDP, 2022).
Within two years of establishing the initiative, the following results were observed:
15 off-grid solar-powered water purification units were installed, providing safe drinking water to over 1,500 people (UNDP, 2022, p. 2; UNDP, 2025, para. 7)
6 ecotourism facilities were built, creating new income streams for 128 households (UNDP, 2022, p. 2)
1,000+ people were trained, including over 50% women, through programs on solar PV maintenance and ecotourism management (UNDP, 2021, para. 4) (UNDP, 2022, p. 2)
Community water management systems were established with elected local committees

However, the change went beyond infrastructure; it reshaped relationships, livelihoods, and hope. Clean water did not arrive in trucks; it flowed from solar-powered purification units managed by village committees, cutting hours from women’s daily routines and dramatically lowering waterborne illness. Ecotourism was not outsourced; it was built from the ground up. Wetland trails were restored by local communities, birdwatching shelters were crafted using traditional materials, and women were trained not only as hosts but also as nature guides fluent in the region’s fragile ecosystem. Skills training was not limited to maintenance; it included budgeting, community planning, and co-managing services, allowing women to step into roles once reserved for elders or men. That is how trust was built, not by delivering services but by embedding responsibility (UNDP, 2022) (UNDP, 2025).

Challenges included maintaining infrastructure in remote areas, navigating post-conflict governance, and addressing deeply entrenched gender norms. These were not solved through top-down delivery but rather through a lengthy process of community dialogue and shared design. Local technicians were trained not only in solar system upkeep but also in troubleshooting with minimal tools, enabling quick fixes without relying on city-based contractors. Governance gaps were addressed by forming elected community committees, which ensured transparency in decisions regarding water access and revenue from ecotourism facilities.

A gender analysis conducted in the Al Hawizeh marshlands informed the project’s design and delivery methods. Key findings are summarized above. Source: (UNDP, 2022).
To address gender barriers, women-only training sessions were held at hours compatible with caregiving responsibilities, and women leaders from nearby areas were invited to mentor new trainees. This was not a one-time intervention but a layered, long-term investment in capacity and trust that allowed communities to take charge of their systems (UNDP Iraq, 2020).
After overcoming these implementation challenges, the project delivered results along three main dimensions:
Water Security: Solar-powered purification units tackled both scarcity and waterborne disease
Resilient Livelihoods: Nature-based tourism offers sustainable income
Empowered Communities: Local training built capacity and trust, especially among women

As Iraq expands this model through its national forest and climate strategies, the lesson is clear: climate solutions, especially in fragile contexts, must serve both people and the planet. In addition to providing electricity, solar panels contributed to improved safety, stability, and daily living conditions. In Al Hawizeh, they illuminated classrooms, powered clean water systems, and returned hours of unpaid labor to women now trained as energy leaders. The impact in Al Hawizeh shows that resilience does not require massive infrastructure; it requires relevance.

What worked here was not just clean energy but also how it was delivered through community-led planning, locally trained technicians, and solutions tailored to real-world conditions. Key lessons include the importance of pairing infrastructure with governance, training with ownership, and technology with trust (UNDP Iraq, 2020). For fragile, climate-affected regions, this model provides a replicable approach that strengthens both human security and local leadership through climate action. Iraq is now applying the same principles across other marshland regions, demonstrating that when solutions are co-owned and context-driven, they are more effective (UNDP, 2022).

Biodiversity Preservation and Nature-Positive Infrastructure
While large-scale renewable projects require significant land, they avoid the most destructive negative externalities of the fossil fuel life cycle, such as open-pit mining, oil spills, and the massive water consumption of thermal cooling systems.18 The emerging paradigm of "Nature-Inclusive Design" (NID) seeks to integrate ecological restoration directly into energy projects.
In the Netherlands and the UK, offshore wind turbine foundations are being designed as artificial reefs to support marine biodiversity and ecosystem functions. On land, "conservoltaic" or "ecovoltaic" solar parks restore native habitats, such as tallgrass prairies, beneath panels, providing a refuge for pollinators and native flora. In Brazil, the target of restoring 12 million hectares of forest as a natural climate solution is expected to create 1 million to 2.5 million jobs, demonstrating the synergy between ecosystem health and economic development.

content.title: Environmental Co-benefits and the Planetary Health Dividend

content.text:
The environmental narrative of sustainable energy has shifted from one of long-term climate mitigation to one of immediate, localized benefits for ecosystems and public health. For developing nations, the transition to renewables is not merely about greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction but about addressing the "triple planetary crisis" of climate change, pollution, and biodiversity loss.
Air Quality and the Mitigation of Respiratory Health Burdens
Energy production is the dominant source of anthropogenic air pollution, which stands as the leading environmental risk factor for global health. In 2021, exposure to fine particulate matter was linked to approximately 6.4 million premature deaths, with the vast majority occurring in low- and middle-income countries. Fossil fuel combustion for power, industry, and transport releases a cocktail of pollutants, including sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and heavy metals like mercury.
The replacement of coal-fired plants and diesel generators with solar, wind, and hydropower provides an immediate health dividend. In China, transitioning to a renewable-heavy scenario could avoid 0.6 million premature deaths and 151 million morbidities annually by 2050.14 Similarly, in Pakistan, air pollution is estimated to drain almost 6% of annual GDP due to lost productivity and healthcare expenditures; for such nations, renewables offer a strategic pathway to save thousands of lives and redirect billions of rupees toward innovation and education.

The 2025 Lancet Countdown report describes this shift as the "greatest global health opportunity of the 21st century," noting that failure to transition has led to 2.52 million annual deaths from outdoor fossil fuel pollution and 2.3 million from "dirty" household fuels.
Similarly, clean cooking is key to addressing indoor air pollution, as seen in Module 2 on Energy Access. Traditional biomass 💬️ and kerosene use release black carbon, a major contributor to indoor air pollution and severe respiratory illnesses, particularly in low-income households. Transitioning to cleaner energy sources for both electricity and cooking can significantly improve public health and reduce environmental harm.

Water Use and Quality
Water use is another important issue when it comes to energy generation. Most energy systems rely on water for cooling and steam production. In 2021, global energy generation used about 370 billion cubic meters of freshwater, equating to 10% of worldwide freshwater withdrawals. Fossil fuel power plants were responsible for a large portion of this water use. Coal plants alone withdrew 189.6 billion cubic meters of water. In contrast, renewable energy technologies used just 12.1 billion cubic meters in 2021. As such, solar panels and wind turbines do not require water for cooling or steam production, using it only for cleaning and construction, significantly reducing overall water consumption. However, geothermal energy 💬️ does require water as a heat transfer fluid in the form of steam or hot water to generate electricity or provide direct heating, making its water use higher than other renewables.

Renewable energy also benefits water quality. Fossil fuel power plants often discharge harmful pollutants like arsenic, mercury, and lead into nearby water bodies, even after wastewater treatment. A 2020 study estimated that, if renewables make up 85% of global energy by 2050, energy-generated freshwater eutrophication (overaccumulation of nutrients in water) would be ten times lower than in a scenario where renewables only comprise 20% of global energy. Marine eutrophication, another major environmental issue, would also be reduced by 3.5 times.

In this lesson, we will explore five key renewable energy technologies that are playing a pivotal role in climate mitigation and shaping the global energy transition. While there are numerous emerging and nascent technologies on the horizon, the focus here will be on those that are already having a significant impact or show strong potential to drive the transition to a low-carbon future. Understanding these technologies is crucial for advancing sustainable energy solutions and achieving the goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and limiting global warming.
